transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, they brought me in. My family, I mean. My brother drove the truck, wouldn't even let me take my own truck, which is ridiculous because I've been driving that Ford since '98 and it runs just fine if you know how to talk to it. But no, they insisted. It was because of the county fair. See, I was giving my talk—I always give a talk about soil rotation and the new fertilizer yields, it’s important, people need to know, the whole county relies on it. But this time, well, I had to show them. Words weren't enough, you know? I had to show them the new pattern. So I climbed right up onto the big John Deere they had on display. Brand new model, beautiful machine. I got up in the cab and I just started working the controls, jerking the levers back and forth, really putting my shoulder into it, because the crowd needed to see the exact rhythm of the pattern. It's all about the rhythm, you see. And they started yelling at me—the fair organizers, my brother, some folks from the feed store—yelling for me to get down, but I couldn't. I just couldn't make myself stop. My hands were moving and the pattern was so clear in my head, I had to finish showing them, even with everyone making such a racket. So, that's why they dragged me down here today.
Has something like this happened to you before?

Well, you know, it hasn't always been like this. I mean, I've always been a hard worker, always had a lot of energy when it comes to the farm, but this... this specific kind of thing, where the patterns get so loud in my head and I just have to show people, that's newer. I'd say it started, oh, maybe about a year and two months ago? Give or take a week or so. It was right around the time we refinanced the whole operation. You see, the bank was being real difficult, asking for all these projections, and my brother was getting nervous, so we decided to do a big farm readjustment. We changed the crop rotation, sold off some of the older equipment—which I told them was a mistake, you don't just sell a good disc harrow because it's a little rusty—and started looking into these new high-yield fertilizers. And ever since then, ever since we started that whole readjustment process, it's like my brain just shifted gears. I started seeing how everything connects, the soil, the seeds, the weather, the machinery... it all makes this perfect, intricate pattern. And it's been going on like that for the last fourteen months, just building and building until, well, until the John Deere incident at the fair. I just had to make them understand what I've been seeing for the past year and a bit.
When you say the patterns get loud in your head, are you hearing actual voices or sounds?

Well, it's... it's not just the patterns getting loud, though they do, they get real loud like a tractor engine revving right in your ear. But yes, since you're asking about voices, it's not just thoughts. It's real. Especially when I'm out by the north pasture. You know the north pasture? It's the one we had to re-grade back in '05 because the drainage was all wrong and the winter wheat kept drowning. Anyway, out there, right around dusk—and it has to be dusk, when the light gets all long and orange across the dirt and the shadows stretch out from the fence posts—I hear them. Clear as day. Or, well, clear as dusk, I suppose. 

They come right up out of the irrigation lines. The aluminum pipes, you know? It's like the metal itself is talking. And it's not just mumbling, it's specific. These voices, they tell me exactly which rows are poisoned and which ones are blessed. They'll say, "Row 42, blight in the roots, poisoned," or "Row 18, the nitrogen took, blessed." And the thing is, Doc, it's not just when I'm feeling all fired up and energetic and my thoughts are racing like a runaway combine. No, sir. Even on the quiet weeks, the weeks when I'm just dragging my boots through the mud and feeling lower than a snake's belly, not a drop of that extra energy in me, I still hear them. I'll be out there checking the couplings, feeling completely drained, and the pipes will still start whispering about the poison in the soil. My brother thinks it's just the wind in the pipes, but the wind doesn't know about soil alkalinity, now does it? The wind doesn't know which rows are blessed.
When you're talking about these patterns and the voices, do you feel like your thoughts are connected and make sense to you, or do they sometimes feel disjointed or hard to follow?

Well, to me, they make perfect sense. Complete sense. Because I see the whole picture, you know? But... well, I suppose when I try to explain it to other people, that's where the trouble starts. Like with my brother, or the men down at the bank. I'll start trying to lay out the plan for them, the real plan, the one the patterns show me. And I'll start talking about the soil carbon levels, because you have to start with the carbon, that's the foundation of everything. But then, you see, the carbon is directly tied to what the bank men are doing with the interest rates, which connects right back up to the weather satellites. They're watching the moisture in the topsoil from space, and that affects the seed genetics we're getting from the supplier. 

And then, before I know it, I'm explaining how the county politics and the zoning board are interfering with the nitrogen cycle in the south field, and... well, people just stare at me. My brother, he'll just throw his hands up and say, "What on earth are you talking about? I asked if we needed to order more diesel!" And I try to tell him, the diesel is part of the satellite grid, but he says my words just get all tangled up like a bird's nest in a combine header. He says I start on one thing and end up somewhere completely different, and I never actually answer the question he asked in the first place. But it's all connected, Doc. It's just... maybe the connections are too fast for them to follow. Or maybe I just have so much of the pattern in my head at once that it all tries to come out of my mouth at the same time, and it just gets... jammed up in the chute.
Do you feel like you're able to express your thoughts in a way that others can understand most of the time?

Well, no, not most of the time. Not lately, anyway. I mean, I try, I really do. Like I was just saying, I'll be trying to explain the plan, the real plan that the patterns show me, and it just... it comes out all tangled up. It's like I'm trying to hand them a perfectly good bale of hay, but by the time it reaches them, the twine's snapped and it's just loose straw blowing everywhere. 

I'll start off simple enough, talking about the soil carbon levels, because you have to understand the soil carbon before you can understand anything else about the farm. It's the bedrock of the whole operation. But then, to explain the carbon, I have to explain what the bank men are doing with the interest rates, because they're squeezing us, and that squeeze is directly tied to the weather satellites. They're up there, watching the moisture in the topsoil, feeding that data back, and that changes the seed genetics we get from the supplier in Omaha. And you can't talk about the seed genetics without bringing in the county politics and the zoning board, because they're the ones interfering with the nitrogen cycle in the south field with that new runoff ordinance they passed last spring. 

So I'm trying to lay all this out, trying to show them how the carbon and the bank and the satellites and the genetics and the politics are all just different cogs in the same big machine, and... and they just look at me like I'm speaking Greek. My brother, he'll ask me something simple, like if we need to order more diesel for the tractors, and I'll start explaining how the diesel fits into the satellite grid, and he just gets so frustrated. He says I never get back to the question he actually asked. He says I just go off on these wild goose chases and leave him standing there wondering if he should call the co-op or not. It's just... it's all so clear in my head, Doc, every single connection, but the minute I open my mouth, it's like trying to pour a whole silo of grain through a garden hose. It just backs up and spills everywhere, and nobody understands what I'm trying to give them.
Do you feel like you're able to stay focused on one topic when you're talking about these patterns and connections?

Well, see, that’s the rub, Doc. Staying on one topic... it’s like trying to lasso a single raindrop in a hurricane. I try, I really do try to just talk about the one thing, especially when my brother is standing there waiting for an answer, but my head... my head just runs so incredibly fast. I mean, impossibly fast, like an engine running completely away from you with the throttle stuck wide open. 

I’ll sit down trying to focus on just the planting schedules—you know, trying to figure out if we’re doing the soybeans in the east 40 or sticking to the winter wheat rotation, which is a whole mess on its own because the frost came late last year and the ground was too hard for too long—but before I can even finish that one single thought about the wheat, the market prices are already rushing in. I'm suddenly thinking about the Chicago Board of Trade, the corn futures, the way the numbers go up and down and how the bank men are manipulating those exact figures to squeeze us out. And then, bam, before the market prices even settle, the soil readings hit me. I'm seeing the pH balances, the nitrogen depletion in the loam, the core samples we took back in April, all of it just flooding my brain at the exact same time. 

And right in the middle of all that dirt and all those numbers, there are the messages. The ones I need to decode from the patterns, the things the pipes and the satellites are trying to warn me about the poisoned rows. It's just... it's a stampede up there. I literally cannot catch one thought before the next one just shoves it completely aside. I reach for the thought about the planting schedule, and the market price thought tackles it, and then the soil reading thought runs right over both of them, and then I'm trying to decode a message about the nitrogen cycle. How is a man supposed to stay focused on one topic when his own mind won't even let him hold onto a thought for more than a split second before the next one comes tearing through?
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to take care of your daily tasks or responsibilities on the farm since these patterns and voices started?

Well, it’s... it’s a hard thing for a man to admit, Doc. A really hard thing, especially when your name is on the deed and you’ve been working that dirt your entire life. I've been running this place, making every single call from seed to harvest, for decades. But lately... well, my wife and the workers, they’ve had to step in and just completely take over the decisions I used to handle. It's like I've been benched on my own property. 

I used to be the one sitting down with the lenders, going over the operating loans and the interest rates for the season. I knew every number backwards and forwards. But now, Mary—my wife—she’s the one talking to the bank men, because... well, they say it just doesn't feel safe with me in charge of that anymore. And it's not just the money. It's the equipment use, too. We’re talking about half-million-dollar machines, the big combines, the heavy tractors. You have to be dialed in when you're running that kind of iron, but with my head running so fast, with the patterns and everything else I'm trying to keep track of, the boys don't want me behind the wheel. They say the daily farm operations just aren't safe if I'm the one calling the shots or running the gear. So they just... they do it themselves. 

And I suppose I can't entirely blame them, not after what happened at the fair. The county fair incident... that was really the turning point, I think. That’s when the whispers really started. I was just trying to get folks to see the connections, trying to explain how the livestock judging was being influenced by the same things affecting the topsoil and the bank rates, but... well, it caused a massive scene right there in front of half the county. Ever since that fair incident, it’s like a switch flipped. It made people—my family, the hands, even the neighbors—it made them all question whether I could keep running the farm at all. They look at me now like I’m some rusted-out old plow that needs to be parked out back behind the barn. I try to tell them I just need to get the patterns sorted, but they’ve just taken the reins right out of my hands, Doc. Every single day, I wake up and watch other men doing my work, making my decisions, and it just... it eats at a man. It really does.
Do you feel like these patterns and voices are interfering with your relationships with your family or the people you work with on the farm?

Interfering? Well, I suppose that's one word for it, Doc. It's more like taking a sledgehammer to a pane of glass, if you really want to get down to the brass tacks of it. It’s tearing the whole fabric of this family right down the middle, and the worst part is, half the time I don't even realize how bad it's getting until the damage is already done. 

See, it’s not just the patterns themselves, it’s... it’s how I feel when I’m seeing them, how my whole body and mind react. Some mornings, I step out onto the back porch, right around dawn when the dew is still heavy on the alfalfa and the sun is just barely cresting the ridge, and I look out over the property, and I just feel... I feel incredible. It's like the whole valley is just opening up for me, presenting itself, showing me every secret it holds. I’ll be standing there, gripping my coffee mug, just grinning at absolutely nothing, feeling like I’ve got the energy of ten men and I can finally fix every single thing that’s broken in this world. I feel ten feet tall, Doc. Untouchable. 

But then... then the reality of the people around me hits, and that's where the friction starts. I’ll walk into the machine shed, riding that high, ready to get the day moving at lightning speed, and one of the hired hands will drag his feet. Or worse, he'll question something I tell him to do. Or Mary, my wife, she’ll come out from the kitchen with that look on her face—you know the one, where her mouth gets all tight and her eyes get sad—and she’ll tell me I need to slow down. Slow down! When I've finally got the momentum to outpace the bank men and the satellites! 

And when they do that, when they question my orders or tell me to put the brakes on... Doc, I just snap. I go from feeling on top of the world to just boiling over in a split second. I snap at them like they've insulted the family name, like they've spit on my father's grave right there in the dirt. I’ll yell, I’ll tell them they’re blind, that they’re dragging us all down to ruin while the whole farm is on the line. I just can't tolerate them holding me back when everything is finally making sense. And then... well, then Mary cries, or she just walks away shaking her head, and the hands start whispering to each other behind the silos, looking at me like I'm a mad dog that needs to be put down. So, yes, it’s interfering. I'm alienating my own wife and the men I rely on to keep this place running, all because they can't keep up with me and I can't stomach their hesitation.
Do you often find yourself jumping from one idea to another when speaking, without finishing your initial thought?

Well, that’s exactly what my brother was yelling about just yesterday morning out by the tool shed. I mean, I try to lay it all out for them, I really do. I’ll get everyone together because I just want to explain the plan, just trying to give them the straight path of what we need to accomplish for the week. But the thing is, you can't just talk about one piece of the farm without talking about the rest of it, because it's all connected, every single moving part. 

But when I open my mouth to explain the plan, it just... it comes out all tangled. Just a tangled mess, like a bad spool of barbed wire that got dropped in the mud. I’ll start off talking about the soil carbon levels—which are completely out of whack this year, by the way, and we need to address it—and before I even finish my sentence about the carbon, I'm having to explain how the bank men are factoring that exact thing into our operating loans. And you can't understand what the bank men are doing unless you understand what the satellites are picking up on their imaging, right? So I'm trying to warn the boys about the satellites, and then that ties right into the seed genetics we bought last spring, and how the local county politics are letting these corporations get away with selling us compromised bags. 

It's all one big picture! It's a straight line to me. But I'll be standing there, out of breath, having laid out this entire web so they can finally see the truth of what we're up against, and my brother or the hired hands will just stare at me. Just blank stares. And they always say the exact same thing to me, Doc. They say I never get back to the question they asked. They’ll ask me if we're greasing the combine today, and I end up on county politics and seed genetics, and I never actually finish the initial thought about the grease. The words just can't keep up with how fast the connections are happening in my head, so I just keep jumping to the next thing, and the next thing, and the next thing, and I leave them all standing there in the dust.
Do you have times when your thoughts feel more organized and easier to express, or is it always this challenging for you to convey what's on your mind?

Well, organized... organized is a word you use for a ledger, Doc. Or a tidy little workbench. My mind hasn't been a tidy workbench in a long, long time. I wish I could sit here and tell you there’s a quiet hour, maybe right before bed or first thing in the morning when the house is still, where everything just lines up neat and pretty. But no. No, it’s just a constant, roaring engine up there, running at the redline day and night, burning through fuel. 

My head just runs so incredibly fast. It's like a stampede that's broken the fence line. It's flooded, absolutely flooded, with the planting schedules for the north forty, and then right on top of that, before I can even process the seed varieties, I'm calculating the Chicago Board of Trade market prices for winter wheat. And then come the soil readings—because you know the nitrogen levels are dropping, I can feel it in my boots when I walk the fields, and the agronomist doesn't know a damn thing about what's really happening in the dirt. And then, right in the middle of all that farm data, right when I'm trying to figure out the yield projections, there are the messages. The messages I need to decode, the ones coming through the patterns in the crop rows and the static on the two-way radio in the truck. 

It's just... it's like trying to catch a single raindrop in a hurricane, Doc. I'll reach out in my mind to grab one thought, just to hold onto it long enough to explain it to Mary or the boys, but I can't catch one thought before the next one just violently shoves it aside. It just shoves it right out of the way! So I'm left standing there, trying to talk about the soil readings, but my brain is already three miles down the road decoding the market prices and the messages from the satellites. It never stops. It never, ever stops, not even for a second. I'll lay my head on the pillow at night, thinking maybe, just maybe, the engine will cool down, but then I'm seeing the spreadsheets, the fertilizer ratios, the way the crows are circling the east silo, and it just keeps shoving and shoving and shoving until I feel like my skull is going to crack wide open from the pressure of it all.
Do you find that your difficulty in expressing your thoughts and following a conversation is significantly impacting your daily life and ability to function on the farm?

Impacting it? Doc, it’s... it’s doing a hell of a lot more than just impacting it. It’s practically driven the whole operation right off a cliff, and I’m just sitting in the passenger seat watching it happen. I mean, you work a piece of land for forty years, you know every dip and rise, every rock in the north pasture, and suddenly... suddenly you’re not the one calling the shots anymore. Mary and the boys, the hired hands, they’ve had to step in and take over. They’ve basically taken over all the decisions I used to handle without even breaking a sweat. 

And it hurts, I won't lie to you, it cuts deep to see another man giving orders on your land. But... but I see why they did it. Because when I can't string two sentences together without my brain running off to the satellites or the soil carbon, things get dangerous. The lenders, for one. The bank men called about renewing our operating note, and Mary had to physically take the phone out of my hand because I was rambling about the county politics instead of giving them the yield projections. She handles the books now. And the equipment... Lord, the equipment. We’ve got a half-million-dollar combine sitting in the machine shed, and my own wife told the hands not to let me near the cab. She said it’s just not safe. Me! A man who could rebuild a diesel engine blindfolded by the time I was twenty! But she says daily farm operations aren't safe with me in charge right now, because I get so lost in my head I might drive a tractor straight into the irrigation ditch trying to follow a pattern in the dirt. 

But the real turning point, the thing that really broke the camel's back, was the county fair last month. I don't know if Mary told you about the fair incident. I went down to the ag pavilion, just trying to talk to the other growers, trying to explain the connections, trying to warn them about what I was seeing with the seed genetics and the market manipulation. But I couldn't keep my thoughts straight. The words just came out roaring, and I ended up shouting, jumping from the fertilizer prices to the radio static, waving my arms around, and I knocked over a whole display table... I made a massive scene right there in front of the 4-H kids and the livestock judges. It was a mess. 

After that... after that fair incident, it was like a switch flipped. The whole town, my family, the workers... they all started questioning whether I could even keep running the farm at all. They look at me like I’m a liability on my own property, Doc. Like I'm broken machinery they don't know how to scrap. So, yes. It’s impacting everything. I can't even talk to my own crew without them looking to my wife to see if they should actually listen to me.
Do you have times when these patterns and voices are not present, or are they always there?

You’d think so, wouldn't you, Doc? You’d think if the tractor finally gets put in park, the radio would shut off too. I used to pray for that. But... well, it’s a funny, cruel sort of thing, how it actually works. 

I mean, there was a spell... we had a few quieter weeks, maybe a month or two ago, where the engine up in my head finally stopped redlining. I was just physically and mentally drained. I wasn't feeling all that energized, wasn't feeling grand or like I could take on the whole county single-handed like I usually do when I'm wound up tight. I wasn't pacing the floorboards or trying to organize the hands. I was just sitting out on the back porch, drinking black coffee, just staring out at the frost melting off the equipment. Just quiet. For several weeks, just quiet.

But the thing that really gets me, the thing that makes my blood run cold when I really sit and think about it, is that even when my body was quiet and I didn't have that fire in my belly... the rest of it didn't go away. The patterns were still there. I'd be sitting there on the porch, barely able to muster the energy to tie my own work boots, but I still heard the lines talking. The power lines and the telephone wires running down the county road at the edge of the property, they were still humming and whispering, sending those messages right across the fields. 

And the data... Lord, the data. Mary would leave the ledger out, or the printouts from the yield monitors, just sitting there on the kitchen island. And I'd look at them, not even trying to decode them, but I still knew. I still believed it, plain as day, that the farm data was carrying those hidden warnings. The warnings about the corporations, the soil, the whole setup. Even without the energy, even without the rush... the warnings were still staring right back at me from the spreadsheets. It’s almost worse that way, you know? Because you’re sitting there in the quiet, and you hear the lines talking, and you see the warnings in the numbers, but you don't even have the strength to jump up and warn anybody about it. You're just trapped with it. So, no, Doc. They never really leave. They just... they just wait for me in the quiet.
Do you find it challenging to maintain a coherent train of thought when discussing your patterns and connections?

Challenging? Doc, it’s like trying to unspool a mile of barbed wire that’s been rolled up wrong and left to rust in the rain. You pull on one end, thinking you’ve got a straight line, and suddenly the whole mess is caught on itself, tearing at your gloves. 

When I sit down, say, at the kitchen table, and I actually try to explain the plan—because there is a plan, a massive, interconnected plan that they all need to understand to keep this farm afloat—it just... it comes out so tangled. I’ll start off trying to tell them about the soil carbon levels, right? Because the carbon is the foundation of the whole acreage, it's the lifeblood of the dirt. But you can't talk about the soil carbon without bringing in the bank men, because the bank men are the ones squeezing our operating notes, which forces us into the cheaper seed genetics. And the seed genetics... well, that’s where the satellites come in, monitoring the yield data from orbit, feeding it right back into the county politics. 

It’s all connected, Doc, every single piece of it, from the courthouse to the combine cab! I see the whole web shining right there in front of me, clear as day. But when I open my mouth to lay it out for Mary or the boys, to just give them the simple truth of how the seed genetics and the satellites are being used by the county politicians... it just rushes out all at once in this big knot. It’s a pileup. I'm trying to explain the plan, and it comes out tangled with the soil carbon, the bank men, the satellites, the seed genetics, the county politics... and then Mary will just look at me, rubbing her temples, and she'll point out that people say I never get back to the question they asked. I’ll realize she’d only asked me what time the feed truck was arriving, and I'm off halfway across the county in my head. I get so far down the line trying to explain the connections that I just leave them standing there in the dust, and I never, ever get back to the question they actually asked me.
Do you feel like the voices and patterns are less prominent or easier to manage when you're not feeling overly energetic or rushed?

Easier to manage? Less prominent? Doc, I wish... I really, truly wish that was how it worked. You’d think without the engine running so hot, the noise would die down, but it doesn't. It really doesn't. 

Take the north pasture, for instance. I can be having one of those weeks where I’m just completely drained, where I'm not all fired up or rushed, just dragging my boots through the dirt and barely keeping my head up. But if I'm out by the north pasture... especially right around dusk, when the sun starts dipping behind the tree line and the shadows get long over the soil... it doesn't matter how tired I am. I'll be out there, maybe checking the pivot, and I will hear them. Clear as a bell, Doc. Clear voices coming straight out of the irrigation lines. 

The water pipes themselves start talking to me. And they aren't just making noise, they're giving me specific instructions, telling me exactly which rows of the crop are poisoned and which ones are blessed. I’ll just be standing there in the fading light, completely exhausted, listening to the aluminum pipes telling me that the third row is tainted and the fifth row is pure, going on and on about the roots and the water supply. 

So, no, the lack of energy doesn't make them less prominent at all. It still happens on weeks when I'm not all fired up... the only difference is I'm just too damn tired to go out and dig up the poisoned rows like I normally would when I've got the energy. The voices are just as loud, just as clear. I'm just... I'm just a captive audience at that point, standing out there in the twilight, listening to the irrigation lines dictate the fate of the harvest while I can barely keep my eyes open.
Do the voices and patterns ever completely stop, or are they always present in some form?

Doc, didn't I... I feel like we just walked down this exact row not ten minutes ago. Like I was saying before, no, they don't ever just pack up and leave. I wish to God they did, but they don't. 

It’s like... well, it's like the dust during a dry harvest. You can shut all the windows in the farmhouse, you can caulk the frames, you can have Mary run that fancy air purifier she bought from the catalog until the filter is black as pitch, but you’re still going to wipe your thumb across the kitchen table and find grit. It’s just always there. 

I’ve tried to find a place where it stops. I really have. I’ve gone right down into the root cellar, thinking maybe under the earth, under all that packed dirt and fieldstone, the signals wouldn't be able to reach me. I went down there and sat on an overturned bucket right among the mason jars—Mary’s got shelves and shelves of them, peaches and green beans, all lined up in the dark on these wooden racks I built her years ago. I sat there in the pitch black, just breathing in that damp earth smell, just begging the Lord for one single minute of real, honest-to-goodness silence. But even down there, Doc, even buried under the house... the glass jars started humming. Just a tiny vibration at first, and then the glass itself started whispering about the frost dates and the corporate buyouts, same as the power lines do. 

So, no. Like I told you, they never completely stop. They might change shape, or they might change volume depending on how much gas is in my tank, but they are always, always running in the background. I don't know how else to explain it to you so it sticks, but that's the truth of it. They're just always there.
Have you ever had a period of time where these voices and patterns completely stopped, only to return later?

Doc, I... I feel like you're just asking me the same question in a different hat, hoping I'll give you a different answer. I just told you, they don't stop. Not down in the root cellar, not out in the fields. They don't take a vacation and come back later. 

It’s been a constant, steady stream. If I really sit back and reckon the days... it started right around the time we were pulling the winter wheat last year. So, let's see, that would make it... about eleven months. Eleven months of this. Eleven months of the voices in the pipes, the coded warnings in the seed catalogs, the humming in the glass jars. 

I remember exactly when it started, too. It was a Tuesday, and I was out by the tractor shed, trying to swap out a busted hydraulic hose on the John Deere. The old green beast was leaking fluid all over the gravel, making this awful dark stain, and I was up to my elbows in grease, just trying to get the fitting threaded right. And that's when the radio in the cab—which wasn't even turned on, mind you, the key was in my pocket—started broadcasting these... these coordinates. Just numbers and letters, over and over, warning me about the soil testing guys from the county. 

And from that Tuesday on, for eleven solid months, it hasn't stopped once. Not for a day, not for an hour. So no, there hasn't been a period where it all just went quiet and then came back. It started eleven months ago by the tractor shed, and it’s been running like a pump motor ever since, day and night, rain or shine. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you, Doc, but it’s been eleven months of non-stop noise.
Have you ever felt like you lost touch with reality?

Lost touch with reality? Doc, I... I have to tell you, it feels like exactly the opposite. It feels like I'm the only one who actually has a firm grip on what's really happening out there. I'm the only one with my eyes wide open to it. 

Take my wife, Mary. Bless her heart, she’s a good woman, a hard worker, but she just... she refuses to see it. She’ll sit me down at the kitchen table, right there on the oak wood her daddy planed himself forty years ago, and she’ll spread out all the lender's paperwork. She’ll smooth out the pages and point at the paragraphs, telling me over and over that it’s just plain paperwork. She tells me it's just standard loan terms for the new equipment, just the regular bank stuff we sign every single year. She desperately wants it to just be normal, just a regular Tuesday evening going over the books.

But I know better. I can't just ignore what's right in front of me, no matter how much she cries about it. I'll go into the office and bring out the yield maps from the last harvest, and those new drone reports the county extension office had done over the south fields back in April. And when you lay them side by side with the bank papers... Doc, it's not just farming data. It's not.

patient.answer:
Impacting it? Doc, it’s... it’s doing a hell of a lot more than just impacting it. It’s practically driven the whole operation right off a cliff, and I’m just sitting in the passenger seat watching it happen. And it hurts, I won't lie to you, it cuts deep to see another man giving orders on your land. But... but I see why they did it. Because when I can't string two sentences together without my brain running off to the satellites or the soil carbon, things get dangerous. The lenders, for one. But the real turning point, the thing that really broke the camel's back, was the county fair last month. I don't know if Mary told you about the fair incident. I went down to the ag pavilion, just trying to talk to the other growers, trying to explain the connections, trying to warn them about what I was seeing with the seed genetics and the market manipulation. After that... after that fair incident, it was like a switch flipped. The whole town, my family, the workers... they all started questioning whether I could even keep running the farm at all. They look at me like I’m a liability on my own property, Doc. Like I'm broken machinery they don't know how to scrap. So, yes. It’s impacting everything. You’d think so, wouldn't you, Doc? You’d think if the tractor finally gets put in park, the radio would shut off too. I used to pray for that. But... well, it’s a funny, cruel sort of thing, how it actually works. 

I mean, there was a spell... we had a few quieter weeks, maybe a month or two ago, where the engine up in my head finally stopped redlining. I was just physically and mentally drained. I wasn't feeling all that energized, wasn't feeling grand or like I could take on the whole county single-handed like I usually do when I'm wound up tight. I wasn't pacing the floorboards or trying to organize the hands. I was just sitting out on the back porch, drinking black coffee, just staring out at the frost melting off the equipment. Just quiet. For several weeks, just quiet.

But the thing that really gets me, the thing that makes my blood run cold when I really sit and think about it, is that even when my body was quiet and I didn't have that fire in my belly... the rest of it didn't go away. The patterns were still there. I'd be sitting there on the porch, barely able to muster the energy to tie my own work boots, but I still heard the lines talking. The power lines and the telephone wires running down the county road at the edge of the property, they were still humming and whispering, sending those messages right across the fields. 

And the data... Lord, the data. Mary would leave the ledger out, or the printouts from the yield monitors, just sitting there on the kitchen island. And I'd look at them, not even trying to decode them, but I still knew. I still believed it, plain as day, that the farm data was carrying those hidden warnings. The warnings about the corporations, the soil, the whole setup. Even without the energy, even without the rush... the warnings were still staring right back at me from the spreadsheets. It’s almost worse that way, you know? Because you’re sitting there in the quiet, and you hear the lines talking, and you see the warnings in the numbers, but you don't even have the strength to jump up and warn anybody about it. You're just trapped with it. So, no, Doc. They never really leave. They just... they just wait for me in the quiet.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a significant reduction in symptoms when not experiencing the high-energy, racing thoughts state
doctor.question: Do you feel like the voices and patterns are less prominent or easier to manage when you're not feeling overly energetic or rushed?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Out by the north pasture, especially near dusk, I hear clear voices coming from the irrigation lines telling me which rows are poisoned or blessed, and it still happens on weeks when I'm not all fired up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the voices and whether they occur when the patient is not feeling energetic ('not all fired up'), which directly aligns with the manifestation of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Easier to manage? Less prominent? Doc, I wish... I really, truly wish that was how it worked. You’d think without the engine running so hot, the noise would die down, but it doesn't. It really doesn't. 

Take the north pasture, for instance. I can be having one of those weeks where I’m just completely drained, where I'm not all fired up or rushed, just dragging my boots through the dirt and barely keeping my head up. But if I'm out by the north pasture... especially right around dusk, when the sun starts dipping behind the tree line and the shadows get long over the soil... it doesn't matter how tired I am. I'll be out there, maybe checking the pivot, and I will hear them. Clear as a bell, Doc. Clear voices coming straight out of the irrigation lines. 

The water pipes themselves start talking to me. And they aren't just making noise, they're giving me specific instructions, telling me exactly which rows of the crop are poisoned and which ones are blessed. I’ll just be standing there in the fading light, completely exhausted, listening to the aluminum pipes telling me that the third row is tainted and the fifth row is pure, going on and on about the roots and the water supply. 

So, no, the lack of energy doesn't make them less prominent at all. It still happens on weeks when I'm not all fired up... the only difference is I'm just too damn tired to go out and dig up the poisoned rows like I normally would when I've got the energy. The voices are just as loud, just as clear. I'm just... I'm just a captive audience at that point, standing out there in the twilight, listening to the irrigation lines dictate the fate of the harvest while I can barely keep my eyes open.

patient.answer:
Doc, didn't I... I feel like we just walked down this exact row not ten minutes ago. Like I was saying before, no, they don't ever just pack up and leave. I wish to God they did, but they don't. 

It’s like... well, it's like the dust during a dry harvest. You can shut all the windows in the farmhouse, you can caulk the frames, you can have Mary run that fancy air purifier she bought from the catalog until the filter is black as pitch, but you’re still going to wipe your thumb across the kitchen table and find grit. It’s just always there. 

I’ve tried to find a place where it stops. I really have. I’ve gone right down into the root cellar, thinking maybe under the earth, under all that packed dirt and fieldstone, the signals wouldn't be able to reach me. I went down there and sat on an overturned bucket right among the mason jars—Mary’s got shelves and shelves of them, peaches and green beans, all lined up in the dark on these wooden racks I built her years ago. I sat there in the pitch black, just breathing in that damp earth smell, just begging the Lord for one single minute of real, honest-to-goodness silence. But even down there, Doc, even buried under the house... the glass jars started humming. Just a tiny vibration at first, and then the glass itself started whispering about the frost dates and the corporate buyouts, same as the power lines do. 

So, no. Like I told you, they never completely stop. They might change shape, or they might change volume depending on how much gas is in my tank, but they are always, always running in the background. I don't know how else to explain it to you so it sticks, but that's the truth of it. They're just always there.

patient.answer:
Doc, I... I feel like you're just asking me the same question in a different hat, hoping I'll give you a different answer. I just told you, they don't stop. Not down in the root cellar, not out in the fields. They don't take a vacation and come back later. 

It’s been a constant, steady stream. If I really sit back and reckon the days... it started right around the time we were pulling the winter wheat last year. So, let's see, that would make it... about eleven months. Eleven months of this. Eleven months of the voices in the pipes, the coded warnings in the seed catalogs, the humming in the glass jars. 

I remember exactly when it started, too. It was a Tuesday, and I was out by the tractor shed, trying to swap out a busted hydraulic hose on the John Deere. The old green beast was leaking fluid all over the gravel, making this awful dark stain, and I was up to my elbows in grease, just trying to get the fitting threaded right. And that's when the radio in the cab—which wasn't even turned on, mind you, the key was in my pocket—started broadcasting these... these coordinates. Just numbers and letters, over and over, warning me about the soil testing guys from the county. 

And from that Tuesday on, for eleven solid months, it hasn't stopped once. Not for a day, not for an hour. So no, there hasn't been a period where it all just went quiet and then came back. It started eleven months ago by the tractor shed, and it’s been running like a pump motor ever since, day and night, rain or shine. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you, Doc, but it’s been eleven months of non-stop noise.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a complete break from reality
doctor.question: Have you ever felt like you lost touch with reality?

target_item.manifestation: Even when my wife shows me the lender's plain paperwork, I know the odd numbers in the yield maps and the drone reports are coded warnings that folks are trying to take the farm out from under me.

patient.answer:
Lost touch with reality? Doc, I... I have to tell you, it feels like exactly the opposite. It feels like I'm the only one who actually has a firm grip on what's really happening out there. I'm the only one with my eyes wide open to it. 

Take my wife, Mary. Bless her heart, she’s a good woman, a hard worker, but she just... she refuses to see it. She’ll sit me down at the kitchen table, right there on the oak wood her daddy planed himself forty years ago, and she’ll spread out all the lender's paperwork. She’ll smooth out the pages and point at the paragraphs, telling me over and over that it’s just plain paperwork. She tells me it's just standard loan terms for the new equipment, just the regular bank stuff we sign every single year. She desperately wants it to just be normal, just a regular Tuesday evening going over the books.

But I know better. I can't just ignore what's right in front of me, no matter how much she cries about it. I'll go into the office and bring out the yield maps from the last harvest, and those new drone reports the county extension office had done over the south fields back in April. And when you lay them side by side with the bank papers... Doc, it's not just farming data. It's not. 

The odd numbers in those yield maps, the specific decimal points in the drone reports... they aren't just measuring crop density or soil moisture. They are coded warnings. I sit there and I try to show her, I really do. I take my pen and I circle the odd numbers, I show her the pattern, how they line up perfectly to spell out what's actually going on behind our backs. It’s a clear warning that folks are trying to take the farm out from under me. 

The lenders, the corporate guys, the soil inspectors... they are all communicating right out in the open through the agricultural data, setting up a squeeze play to force me off my land. My grandfather cleared this land, Doc. I'm not about to let them just take it. 

So no, I haven't lost touch with reality. The reality is that there is a coordinated effort to steal my livelihood, and I'm the only one standing in the gap. If I just smiled and nodded at Mary's plain paperwork like a blind fool, they'd have padlocks on my gates by the first frost. I'm more in touch with reality than anyone else in that house. I have to be, or we'll lose everything.

patient.answer:
Well, no, Doc. No, I wouldn't say that at all. A different world? That makes it sound like I'm off floating in the clouds somewhere, or living in some kind of dream. But I'm not. I'm right here. We are all standing on the exact same dirt, breathing the exact same air. 

I mean, take just the other morning. I drove the pickup down to Miller’s Feed and Seed right off Highway 9, same as I do most weeks. I walked in, and you get that heavy smell of sweet feed and alfalfa dust right in your nose—you know the smell, it just settles into the denim of your jeans and stays there. I went over to the corner where they keep that old Bunn coffee maker, the one that always burns the bottom quarter of the pot so it tastes like battery acid, and I poured myself a cup. I’m standing there with Tom, the manager, and a couple of the other guys from the eastern ridge. We’re all in the exact same room, in the exact same world, looking at the exact same chalkboard where Tom writes up the daily seed prices. 

There’s no alternate reality about it. The difference is just... well, it's just that I'm actually paying attention to what's going on in this world. Tom is standing there complaining about the freight costs for soybean meal, just looking at the surface of things. But I’m looking at the board, and I can see how the fractions in those prices match up perfectly with the drone coordinates and the soil testing schedules I was telling you about earlier. It’s right there in white chalk. I even tried to point it out to them. I set my coffee down on the counter—spilled a little bit on a stack of receipts, actually, Mary would have tanned my hide for being clumsy—and I traced the numbers for them. I showed them how the corporate guys are broadcasting the squeeze play right out in the open, right there at the local feed store. 

But they just look at me. They put their blinders on, just like a team of draft horses pulling a heavy wagon down a narrow lane. They don't want to look left or right, they just want to get to the end of the day. So, no, I'm not living in a different world. I'm living in this one, the real one, and it is a hard, dangerous world right now if you own land. I just happen to be the only man standing at the counter who realizes the barn is on fire while everyone else is just complaining about the smoke. Does that make sense? I'm right here in reality. I just don't have the luxury of being blind to it like they do.

Well, see, the thing is... it’s not that I can't stick to a topic. It's just that the topic ain't just one simple thing. It’s... well, it’s everything all tied together, like a massive root ball under an old stump. You pull on one little root, and the whole ground shifts. 

So when someone asks me something, or when I try to sit down and actually explain the plan to them—to really lay out what these folks are doing to take the farm—it just... it comes out tangled. And then you can't grasp the county politics unless you look at the new soil carbon mandates they’ve been pushing on us since last fall. So I have to explain the soil carbon to make the bank stuff make sense. And that naturally leads right into the satellites—because how else are they tracking the carbon? They've got satellites doing overhead imaging of my south acreage every three days, I've tracked the orbits. And those satellite readings, well, they tie directly into the seed genetics the corporate suppliers are trying to force us to plant this spring. 

So I'm laying all this out, just trying to give them the full picture so they can finally see the truth of it—the soil carbon, the bank men, the satellites, the seed genetics, the county politics—and by the time I get the whole web drawn out for them, they just sigh. They rub their eyes and look at the clock. They say I'm rambling, or that I jump around too much, and they always complain that I never get back to the question they asked me in the first place. 

But Doc, how am I supposed to give a short answer to a simple question when the real answer involves half the county, the seed companies, and the sky above us? I'm not losing the topic. No, no, never. Never like that. I mean, if anything, I'm the one who feels the realness of it all too sharply. It's like... like when a cold front moves in and the temperature drops twenty degrees in an hour, and you feel that ache deep in your knuckles? You don't doubt that the cold is real. You feel it in your bones. That's how this is. 

I've never sat there and thought, "Oh, maybe none of this is happening, maybe my mind is playing tricks." Because I can go right out and touch it. I can walk out the back door, past the old rusted diesel tank that’s been sitting there since '98, and I can kneel down and sift the dirt through my fingers. I can smell the rain coming off the hills. I can hold the bank papers in my hands and feel the weight of the paper, trace the ink with my thumb. It's all physical. It's all happening right here on the ground. 

If it wasn't real, if I was just making it up in my head, then why would the yield maps match the feed store prices? Why would the satellite schedules line up perfectly with the days the county assessor drives his white truck past my property line? You can't make up that kind of consistency, Doc. It's too perfectly orchestrated. 

Sometimes I wish it wasn't real. I really do. I'll be sitting on the porch at 3 AM, just watching the tree line, listening to the coyotes yipping down in the draw, and I'll think to myself, "Lord, I wish this was just a bad dream. I wish I could wake up and just worry about rain and rust like my daddy did." But then I'll see the blinking lights of the drones doing their sweeps over the south acreage, and the cold hard reality of it just settles right back onto my shoulders. So no, I've never felt like it wasn't real. It's the most real thing I've ever dealt with in my sixty years on this earth, and I've dealt with a lot of hard realities.
